title: II. Smerdyakov With A Guitar
paragraphs: He really had no time to lose. Even while he was saying good-bye to Lise, it had occurred to him that he would need some trick to catch his brother Dmitri, who was obviously avoiding him. It was getting late, nearly three o’clock. Alyosha’s whole soul pulled him toward the monastery and his dying saint, but the need to see Dmitri outweighed everything. With each hour that passed he grew surer that some great, unavoidable disaster was about to strike. What that disaster was, and what he would say to his brother when it came, he could probably not have said clearly. “Even if my benefactor has to die without me, at least I won’t have to reproach myself for the rest of my life. I won’t have to think that I might have saved something and didn’t, that I walked past and hurried home. If I do what I mean to do, I will be following his great teaching.”

His plan was to take his brother Dmitri by surprise. He would climb the fence as he had the day before, slip into the garden and sit in the summer-house. If Dmitri wasn’t there, Alyosha thought, he would not announce himself to Foma or the women of the house. He would stay hidden in the summer-house, even if that meant waiting until evening. If Dmitri was lying in wait for Grushenka again, as before, he would very likely come to the summer-house. Alyosha did not dwell on the details of the plan, though. He simply decided to carry it out, even at the cost of not getting back to the monastery that day.

Everything went smoothly. He climbed over the hurdle at almost the same spot as the day before and got into the summer-house without being seen. He did not want to be noticed. The woman of the house, and Foma too if he was around, might be loyal to his brother and follow his orders. They might refuse to let Alyosha into the garden, or they might warn Dmitri that somebody was looking for him and asking questions.

The summer-house was empty. Alyosha sat down and began to wait. He looked around, and the place struck him as much older than before. The day was as fine as yesterday’s, yet this time the summer-house looked wretched. A ring was left on the table, no doubt from the glass of brandy spilled the day before. Foolish, pointless thoughts drifted through his head, as they always do during a dull wait. He wondered, for instance, why he had sat in exactly the same spot as before, and not on the other seat. At last he felt very low, worn down by suspense and uncertainty. But he had not been sitting there even a quarter of an hour when he suddenly heard a guitar being strummed very close by. Somewhere in the bushes, not twenty paces off, some people were sitting, or had only just sat down. Alyosha suddenly remembered that when he left the summer-house the day before, he had glimpsed an old, low green garden-seat among the bushes on the left, by the fence. That must be where they were sitting now. Who were they?
A man’s voice suddenly broke into song, in a sugary falsetto, with the guitar to accompany it:
A force I cannot fight has bound me to my dear. O Lord, have mercy on her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
The voice stopped. It was a lackey’s tenor and a lackey’s song. Then a woman’s voice asked, in a coaxing and bashful tone, though with a mincing affectation:
“Why haven’t you come to see us for such a long time, Pavel Fyodorovitch? Why do you always look down on us?”

“Not at all,” a man’s voice answered, politely but with pointed dignity. It was clear that the man had the upper hand and that the woman was making advances. “That must be Smerdyakov,” thought Alyosha, “judging by the voice. And the lady must be the daughter of the house, who has come back from Moscow. The one in the dress with a train, who goes to Marfa for soup.”
“I’m awfully fond of verses of any kind, so long as they rhyme,” the woman’s voice went on. “Why don’t you sing more?”
The man began to sing again:
What do I care for a king’s riches If only my dear one keeps well? Lord, have mercy On her and on me! On her and on me! On her and on me!
“Last time it was even better,” the woman’s voice remarked. “You sang ‘If my darling keeps well,’ and it sounded more tender. I suppose you’ve forgotten it today.”
“Poetry is rubbish!” Smerdyakov said curtly.
“Oh, no! I love poetry.”

“Insofar as it is poetry, it is rubbish through and through. Just think about it: who ever talks in rhyme? And suppose we were all made to talk in rhyme, even by government decree. We wouldn’t say much, would we? Poetry is no use, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“How clever you are! How did you come to go so deep into everything?” The woman’s voice grew more and more coaxing.

“I could have gone further than this. I could have known more, if my fate hadn’t been against me from childhood. I would have shot a man in a duel for calling me names because I come from a filthy beggar and have no father. In Moscow they used to throw that in my teeth. The story had reached them from here, thanks to Grigory Vassilyevitch. Grigory Vassilyevitch accuses me of rebelling against my birth, but I would have agreed to their killing me before I was born, so that I would never have come into the world at all. In the market they used to say it, and your mamma too, with a great lack of delicacy, began telling me that her hair was like a mat on her head and that she was short of five foot by a wee bit. Why say a wee bit when she might have said ‘a little bit,’ like everybody else? She wanted to make it touching, a proper peasant feeling. Can a Russian peasant be said to feel anything, next to an educated man? In his ignorance he can’t be said to have any feeling at all. Since I was a child, whenever I hear ‘a wee bit,’ I nearly burst with rage. I hate all Russia, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“If you’d been an army cadet, or a young hussar, you wouldn’t talk that way. You’d have drawn your saber to defend all Russia.”
“I don’t want to be a hussar, Marya Kondratyevna. What’s more, I’d like to do away with all soldiers.”
“And when an enemy comes, who’s going to defend us?”

“There’s no need for defense. In 1812 Napoleon, first Emperor of the French and father of the present one, made a great invasion of Russia. It would have been a good thing if they had conquered us. A clever nation would have conquered a very stupid one and swallowed it up. We would have ended up with quite different institutions.”

“Are things really so much better in their country than in ours? I wouldn’t trade one dandy I know for three young Englishmen,” said Marya Kondratyevna tenderly, no doubt shooting him a most languishing glance as she said it.
“That depends on what one prefers.”
“But you’re exactly like a foreigner, like a most gentlemanly foreigner. I’m telling you so, though it makes me bashful.”

“If you want to know, the people over there and the people here are alike in their vices. They’re all swindlers. The only difference is that over there the scoundrel wears polished boots, and here he grovels in filth and sees nothing wrong with it. The Russian people need a good thrashing, as Fyodor Pavlovitch said very truly yesterday, mad as he is, and all his children.”
“But you told me yourself you had such respect for Ivan Fyodorovitch.”

“Yet he called me a stinking lackey. He thinks I might turn unruly. There he’s mistaken. If I had a certain sum in my pocket, I’d have left here long ago. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is lower than any lackey in how he behaves, how he thinks and how poor he is. He can’t do anything, and still everyone respects him. I may be only a soup-maker, but with a bit of luck I could open a café restaurant in Petrovka, in Moscow, because my cooking is something special, and in Moscow nobody’s cooking is special except the foreigners’. Dmitri Fyodorovitch is a beggar, but if he challenged the son of the first count in the land, he’d fight him. And yet how is he better than I am? He’s ever so much stupider than I am. Look at all the money he’s thrown away for no reason!”
“A duel must be lovely,” Marya Kondratyevna suddenly remarked.
“How so?”

“It must be so frightening and so brave, especially when young officers with pistols in their hands pop away at each other over some lady. A perfect picture! Ah, if only girls were allowed to watch, I’d give anything to see one!”
“It’s all very well while you’re the one doing the shooting. But when the other fellow is aiming right at your mug, you must feel pretty silly. You’d be glad to run, Marya Kondratyevna.”
“You don’t mean that you would run?” But Smerdyakov did not stoop to reply. After a moment of silence the guitar tinkled again, and in the same falsetto he sang once more:
Say what you like, I’m going far away. Life will be bright and gay In the city far away. I won’t grieve, I won’t grieve at all, I don’t intend to grieve at all.

Then something unexpected happened. Alyosha sneezed. The two fell silent. Alyosha got up and walked over to them. He found Smerdyakov all dressed up, in polished boots, his hair pomaded and perhaps curled. The guitar lay on the garden-seat. His companion was the daughter of the house, in a light-blue dress with a train two yards long. She was young and would not have been bad-looking, except that her face was so round and so terribly freckled.
“Will my brother Dmitri be back soon?” Alyosha asked, as calmly as he could.
Smerdyakov got up slowly, and Marya Kondratyevna rose as well.
“How should I know about Dmitri Fyodorovitch? It isn’t as if I were his keeper,” Smerdyakov answered, quietly, distinctly and with an air of superiority.
“I only asked whether you happen to know,” Alyosha explained.
“I know nothing of where he is, and I don’t wish to.”
“But my brother told me you keep him informed of everything that goes on in the house. He said you’d promised to tell him when Agrafena Alexandrovna comes.”
Smerdyakov turned a slow, unmoved gaze on him.
“And how did you get in this time, when the gate was bolted an hour ago?” he asked, with his eyes on Alyosha.
“I came through the back-alley and over the fence, and went straight to the summer-house. I hope you’ll forgive me,” he added, turning to Marya Kondratyevna. “I was in a hurry to find my brother.”

“Ach, as if we could take offense at you!” drawled Marya Kondratyevna, flattered by Alyosha’s apology. “Dmitri Fyodorovitch often comes into the summer-house that way. We don’t know he’s here, and there he is, sitting in the summer-house.”
“I’m very anxious to find him, or to hear from you where he is now. Believe me, it concerns something very important to him.”
“He never tells us anything,” lisped Marya Kondratyevna.

“I used to come here as a friend,” Smerdyakov began again, “but even here Dmitri Fyodorovitch has hounded me without mercy with his endless questions about the master. ‘What news?’ he’ll ask. ‘What’s going on in there now? Who comes and goes?’ And can’t I tell him something more? Twice already he’s threatened me with death.”
“With death?” Alyosha exclaimed in surprise.

“Do you suppose he’d think twice about it, with his temper, which you had a chance to see for yourself yesterday? He says that if I let Agrafena Alexandrovna in and she spends the night there, I’ll be the first to pay for it. I’m terribly afraid of him. If I weren’t even more afraid of doing it, I ought to tell the police. God only knows what he might do!”
“Just the other day his honor told him, ‘I’ll pound you in a mortar!’” added Marya Kondratyevna.
“Oh, if it’s pounding in a mortar, it may be only talk,” said Alyosha. “If I could meet him, I might talk to him about that too.”

“Well, here is the one thing I can tell you,” said Smerdyakov, as if on second thought. “I’m here as an old friend and neighbor, and it would be strange if I didn’t come. On the other hand, Ivan Fyodorovitch sent me first thing this morning to your brother’s lodging in Lake Street. I had no letter, only a message asking Dmitri Fyodorovitch to dine with him at the restaurant here, in the market-place. I went, but I didn’t find Dmitri Fyodorovitch at home, though it was eight o’clock. ‘He was here, but he’s long gone,’ those were the landlady’s very words. It’s as though the two of them had an understanding. Perhaps at this moment he’s in the restaurant with Ivan Fyodorovitch. Ivan Fyodorovitch hasn’t come home to dinner, you see, and Fyodor Pavlovitch dined alone an hour ago and has gone to lie down. But I beg you most particularly not to say anything about me or what I’ve told you, because he’d kill me for nothing at all.”
“Brother Ivan has invited Dmitri to the restaurant today?” Alyosha repeated quickly.
“Yes, that’s right.”
“The Metropolis tavern, in the market-place?”
“The very one.”
“That’s quite likely,” cried Alyosha, very excited. “Thank you, Smerdyakov. That’s important. I’ll go there at once.”
“Don’t give me away,” Smerdyakov called after him.
“Oh, no. I’ll go into the tavern as if by chance. Don’t worry.”
“But wait a minute, I’ll open the gate for you,” cried Marya Kondratyevna.
“No, it’s a short cut. I’ll go over the fence again.”

What he had heard threw Alyosha into great agitation. He ran to the tavern. He could not go inside in his monastic dress, but he could ask at the entrance for his brothers and call them down. But just as he reached the tavern, a window was thrown open and his brother Ivan called to him from above.
“Alyosha, can’t you come up here? I’d be awfully grateful.”
“Of course I can, only I’m not sure about going in this dress—”
“But I’m in a room by myself. Come up the steps, and I’ll run down to meet you.”
A minute later Alyosha was sitting beside his brother. Ivan was dining alone.
